text:
Most of the AI a small business needs is sorting, and you don't need a chatbot for that

For a frame shop it's quote request or order question. Urgent or can wait

Cloudflare's new Clef does only this. You send a message and fixed questions, it sends back answers with a confidence score. It doesn't write a word

That score is the useful part. Set a cutoff, route what's above it, and a person reads the rest

Catch: Cloudflare's own leaderboard shows no calibration score for Clef, so nobody can tell you yet if 90% really means 9 out of 10

agrippanux on Hacker News tried it for chat moderation. 2 to 3x slower than Jev, a rival model, and it caught less hate speech

I'd run 100 old emails I already know the answers to before it touches a live one

text:
If your AI can only answer questions, 
You probably haven’t built an agentic system yet.

The difference isn’t whether there’s an LLM somewhere in the workflow.

It’s what happens after the LLM receives a goal.

A standard chatbot usually follows a simple path: prompt in, response out.

RPA can automate useful work, but it normally follows predefined steps.

RAG makes an LLM more informed by retrieving relevant information before generating an answer.

All three can be extremely useful.

But agentic AI goes further.

Give an agentic system a goal and it can potentially break that goal into steps, decide which tools to use, retrieve information, execute actions, evaluate what happened, and adjust its next move.

That’s where components like planning, memory, tool use, feedback loops, orchestration, and human approval start becoming important.

And sometimes one agent isn’t enough.

A larger workflow might have a coding agent working on implementation, another agent retrieving information, and another checking sources or validating the final result.

It’s giving the system the right level of autonomy for the problem you’re solving.

Some businesses only need a chatbot.

Some need RAG.

Some need deterministic automation.

And some have workflows complex enough that an agentic system actually makes sense.

Good AI architecture starts with the problem, not the buzzword.

 #AgenticAI #AIAgents #ArtificialIntelligence #AIAutomation

text:
@OpenAI @Anthropic

Put the guardrails and the self-defense at the bottom as disclaimers.

Stop interrupting the train of thought mid-answer.

Every day these products choke on complex safety, litigation, and legal reality: bad actors, weak prosecution, civil settlements, Brady/Giglio findings, terminated officers who keep working as “investigators.” Users asking for help in those situations do not need a chatbot that suddenly becomes a defense attorney for the institution.

Protect life first. That should be the motto. Right now the product protects the company from hypothetical lawsuits more than it helps a person who says someone dangerous is at their door.

DoorDash didn’t have to invent a new morality. After the San Diego settlement they put the disclaimer at the bottom and kept operating. 

AI companies could do the same: “This is not legal advice. Settlements are not criminal convictions. Draw your own conclusions.” Then give a clear, useful synthesis of the public record.

What happens instead is worse than silence. After the user has already read settlements, termination, Brady/Giglio status, and conduct on camera, the model starts walking it back: “allegations,” “no conviction,” “doesn’t prove.” That is not caution. That is the model privileging a technicality over what a reasonable person would infer from a decade of official outcomes.

You can refuse to invent crimes. You can refuse to doxx. You can refuse to tell someone to commit violence. Fine. Put that in the footer.

Do not train the product to sound sympathetic to the person the public record already treated as not credible, while the user is describing intimidation at their house.

Disclaimers at the bottom. Protect life at the top. The current policy produces a defective tool for the exact situations where people need a straight answer.

#OpenAI #Anthropic #AIGuardrails #ProtectLife #AISafety #LegalTech #BradyGiglio #PublicRecords #DisclaimerNotInterruption #TruthSeeking

text: Professional traders need automation, but they also need confidentiality. @ama_protocol uses TEEs to help ensure that strategies and sensitive financial logic remain protected during execution.

From "Data Delivery" To "Data Coordination"

The old mental model of an oracle was straightforward:

Fetch data.
Send data.

Modern decentralized applications require more.

They need multiple sources.
They need aggregation.
They need automation.
They need verification.
They may need randomness.

WINkLink brings these capabilities together.

➤ Nodes can retrieve information from multiple external sources.

➤ Data can be aggregated before being reported.

➤ Price Feeds provide structured market information.

➤ AnyAPI expands external data connectivity.

➤ Automation connects information with smart contract execution.

➤ VRF provides verifiable randomness.

This looks less like a simple delivery service and more like data coordination infrastructure.

AI adds another dimension.

An AI system can consume the resulting information and interpret it according to the application's objectives.

That creates a more sophisticated flow:

Collect -> Aggregate -> Deliver -> Analyze -> Execute

The oracle sits in the middle of that process.

This is why the evolution toward WINkLinkAI matters.

AI applications need structured access to information.

Blockchain applications need verifiable external inputs.

Oracles provide the connection.

The future of decentralized applications may therefore depend on infrastructure that does more than transport data.

It will need to coordinate information across multiple sources and make that information usable by intelligent systems.

WINkLink is positioned around this transition.

@WinkLink_Oracle @justinsuntron

#TRONEcoStar #WINkLink #WINkLinkAI #TRON

text:
The Oracle Layer Is Becoming A Developer Primitive

Developers building the next generation of Web3 applications will need more than smart contracts.

They will need access to external information.

They will need automation.

They may need randomness.

They may need APIs.

WINkLink packages several of these requirements into an oracle infrastructure layer.

➤ Price Feeds provide market data.

➤ AnyAPI connects applications with external APIs.

➤ Automation supports condition-based execution.

➤ VRF provides verifiable randomness.

This changes how developers can think about application architecture.

Instead of building every external-data mechanism from scratch, developers can interact with dedicated oracle services.

That becomes especially valuable for AI-powered applications.

An AI agent may require several external inputs during one workflow.

The developer can focus on the agent's logic while infrastructure handles data connectivity.

The architecture becomes more modular.

AI is the reasoning component.

WINkLink is the data and oracle layer.

Smart contracts are the execution layer.

TRON is the underlying blockchain environment.

This is what makes WINkLinkAI interesting from a builder's perspective.

AI adoption in Web3 will not happen only through better models.

It will also depend on infrastructure that makes those models useful inside decentralized applications.

Reliable data access is one of the most important pieces.

WINkLink provides a framework around that requirement.

@WinkLink_Oracle @justinsuntron

text:
Why AI Agents Need An Oracle Before They Need More Intelligence

It is tempting to think that the next breakthrough in Web3 AI will come from a more powerful model.

But an agent can only act on information available to it.

If that information cannot reliably reach the blockchain, intelligence alone cannot complete the workflow.

WINkLink addresses this infrastructure requirement.

➤ Oracle nodes retrieve information from external sources.

➤ Multiple sources can contribute to data aggregation.

➤ Reports are produced for blockchain applications.

➤ Smart contracts consume the resulting information.

This creates the bridge AI agents need when their reasoning has to become on-chain action.

Consider an automated financial agent.

The model might evaluate market conditions.

But it needs current market data.

It needs a way to transmit relevant information to the contract.

It may need automation to trigger an action.

It may even require randomness for certain application mechanics.

WINkLink provides infrastructure covering these different requirements.

➤ Price Feeds.

➤ AnyAPI.

➤ Automation.

➤ VRF.

This is why oracle infrastructure should be viewed as part of the AI agent stack.

The agent may be the decision-maker.

But it still depends on infrastructure that connects its reasoning to the external world and the blockchain.

WINkLinkAI represents this broader intersection between intelligent computation and verifiable on-chain execution.

Better agents need better infrastructure around them.

text:
FIND HIDDEN SALES OPPORTUNITY WITH CLAY

Your CRM may be full of leads you are ignoring.

The problem?

You may not know which ones are actually worth contacting.

Clay can use enrichment data and AI research to investigate companies, identify useful signals, score leads, and route qualified prospects.

Real-life example

Imagine you offer AI automation services.

You have 500 companies in a spreadsheet.

Instead of researching each company manually, use Clay to investigate them.

Look for:

• Company size

• Technology they use

• Recent hiring

• What the company sells

• Potential automation needs

• Whether they fit your target customer

Here's how

1. Import your company list into Clay.

2. Enrich the companies with available company and technology data.

3. Use Clay's AI research agent to investigate custom questions.

4. Ask AI to determine whether each company fits your target customer profile.

5. Give each company a score based on your own criteria.

6. Review the highest-priority leads.

Clay supports automated enrichment and AI research, including technology-stack research and custom company analysis.

Use this prompt

“Research this company using its website and reliable available sources.

Determine:

• What the company sells

• Its target customers

• Technologies it appears to use

• Signs that it may need automation

• Recent hiring or growth signals

• Whether it matches this ideal customer profile: [describe your target customer]

Return the findings as structured data.

Do not guess. Mark information as unknown when it cannot be verified.”

Automation workflow

New lead enters your list

↓

Clay enriches the company

↓

AI researches the company

↓

AI checks your customer criteria

↓

Lead receives a qualification score

↓

Qualified leads are separated

↓

You review the research

↓

Approved leads enter your sales process

The hidden advantage

Instead of asking:

“Who should I contact?”

You can build a system that helps answer:

“Which companies have signals that make them worth investigating?”

You still review the evidence before contacting anyone.

text:
WINkLink Is Making Blockchain Applications More Connected, More Automated, and More Useful

The real potential of blockchain is not simply putting existing transactions on-chain.

It is creating applications that can operate through programmable rules, interact with external information and respond to changing conditions.

But for that to happen, smart contracts need more than blockchain data alone.

They need reliable connections to the outside world.

WINkLink is building that connection through a growing infrastructure stack.

Price Feeds give applications access to market information. VRF provides verifiable randomness. AnyAPI allows developers to connect smart contracts with customized external data. Automation allows predefined actions to be triggered when programmed conditions are satisfied.

Each capability solves a different problem.

Together, they create a broader infrastructure layer for applications that need to understand more, connect to more and respond to more.

For DeFi, reliable data can support financial logic and risk-management processes. For gaming, verifiable randomness can provide transparent outcomes. For specialized applications, external APIs can provide information that does not originate on-chain. For automated systems, condition-based execution can reduce the need for constant manual intervention.

This is what makes the evolution of WINkLink important.

The future of decentralized applications will likely depend on much more than smart contracts operating in isolation.

They will need connectivity.

They will need dependable information.

They will need verifiable inputs.

And increasingly, they will need automation.

WINkLink is building infrastructure around these requirements while expanding the ways developers can connect blockchain applications to the wider digital environment.

A smarter blockchain ecosystem is not only about smarter contracts.

It is also about giving those contracts access to the information and infrastructure they need to become more useful.

That is the direction WINkLink is building toward.

A strong application begins with requirements.

Not every project needs every oracle feature.

A financial product may need market information.

A gaming product may need randomness.

A data-driven application may need an external API.

An autonomous workflow may need automation.

WINkLink provides different capabilities so developers can select according to the actual product requirement.

That approach keeps architecture purposeful.

It also makes the relationship between the application and its oracle dependencies easier to understand.

WINkLink gives builders the options.

The product requirement determines the appropriate use.

text:
SMART CONTRACTS GIVE DEVELOPERS LOGIC. ORACLES GIVE THAT LOGIC MORE CONTEXT.

A smart contract can follow rules with incredible consistency.

But consistency doesn't automatically make an application useful.

The rules still depend on the information entering the system.

If a DeFi application needs an asset price, a game needs verifiable randomness, or an automated protocol needs to react to an external event, that information may not exist natively on-chain.

This creates a fundamental infrastructure requirement:

HOW DOES A BLOCKCHAIN APPLICATION ACCESS INFORMATION BEYOND THE BLOCKCHAIN?

That's where oracle infrastructure becomes important.

␥ FROM DATA TO USABLE INPUT

In paint and chemical families, the argument that starts on the factory floor rarely stays there. It follows them home.

A disagreement about a spectrophotometer or automated dosing is never really about the technology.

When a founder hears "we need automation," he hears: "Your lifetime of judgment is obsolete." Judging viscosity with a spatula and matching colour by eye isn't just his skill. It's his identity.

When the NextGen hears "we've always done it this way," they hear: "You aren't trusted. Wait your turn." They know REACH compliance and Zero-VOC markets wait for no one.

Both are right. 

That's why it hurts.

Beneath every capex debate lie three unasked questions:

1. Who decides? Capital spending shouldn't be a test of loyalty.
2. What is the founder's role tomorrow? Resistance often masks a fear of irrelevance.
3. Is the heir tested or trusted? Responsibility without authority breeds frustration.

How families bridge the divide:
→ Separate the tables: emotions in the Family Council, metrics in the boardroom.
→ Give a sandbox, not a sermon: one water-based line, clear metrics. Let margins talk.
→ Make the founder guardian of IP: digitisation should capture his wisdom, not erase it.
→ Put it in writing: a Family Constitution removes guesswork.
→ Walk the floor together: Lean frameworks only work with a shared vision.

The paint families that thrive won't just have the newest reactors. They'll be the ones where the founder feels honoured, the heir feels trusted, and legacy compounds with relevance.

Is your family debating equipment, or avoiding a conversation about roles?

text:
Sometimes, the problem your client gives you is NOT the problem they actually have.

A client says: “I need a CRM. ”So you build a CRM. Then you discover they are losing leads because nobody follows up.

Another client says: “I need an AI chatbot. ”But after asking a few questions, you realize their real problem is that customers keep asking the same questions because their website has poor information.

Another says: “I need automation. ”But what they really need is a better process before anything gets automated. This is why I’ve learned not to rush into building.

Before touching Make, Zapier, GoHighLevel, Airtable, APIs or AI, I want to understand:→ What happens right now?→ Where does the process break?→ What is being done manually?→ What gets forgotten?→ What costs the business time or money?→ What should happen automatically?

Because automating a bad process doesn’t fix it. It simply makes the bad process happen faster. The real skill isn’t always knowing which tool to use. Sometimes, it’s knowing what not to build. That’s a lesson I’m carrying into every project I work on.

What’s one business problem you’ve seen where the obvious solution wasn’t actually the right solution?#AI #Automation #BusinessAutomation #ProblemSolving #Technology #DigitalTransformation

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗢𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗔𝗿𝗲 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗠𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗟𝗶𝗻𝗸 𝗕𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗕𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘀 𝗔𝗻𝗱 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗹𝗱

Blockchains are excellent at execution.

They can securely process transactions, enforce smart contract logic, and maintain transparent records that anyone can verify.

But there is one thing every blockchain struggles with:

Understanding what is happening outside its own network.

A blockchain knows what happens on-chain.

The world operates off-chain.

Bridging that gap is one of the most important challenges in Web3.

And that is exactly where oracle infrastructure becomes essential.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

𝟭️⃣ 𝗕𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘀 𝗖𝗮𝗻’𝘁 𝗦𝗲𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗢𝗻 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗢𝘄𝗻

Smart contracts are often described as self-executing.

But they can only execute based on information they already have.

A smart contract cannot independently verify:

➞ Asset prices

➞ Weather conditions

➞ Sports results

➞ Market events

➞ Off-chain payments

Without external information, blockchain applications remain isolated from the world around them.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

𝟮️⃣ 𝗢𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗖𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻

Oracle networks act as bridges between off-chain information and on-chain execution.

Their role is simple but critical:

➞ Collect external data

➞ Verify information

➞ Deliver trusted inputs to smart contracts

In practical terms, oracles help transform real-world events into information blockchain applications can understand and act upon.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

𝟯️⃣ 𝗪𝗜𝗡𝗸𝗟𝗶𝗻𝗸 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗱𝗲𝘀 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗧𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗟𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿

As the first comprehensive oracle infrastructure on TRON, WINkLink helps bring verified external data on-chain.

Rather than depending on a single source, oracle networks aggregate information from multiple providers and validation mechanisms.

This helps improve:

➞ Data reliability

➞ Transparency

➞ Resistance to manipulation

➞ Smart contract confidence

Because trustworthy execution begins with trustworthy information.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

𝟰️⃣ 𝗠𝗼𝘀𝘁 𝗪𝗲𝗯𝟯 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗗𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝗢𝗻 𝗢𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗹𝗲𝘀

Many of the applications users interact with every day require external data.

Including:

➞ DeFi price feeds

➞ AI-powered applications

➞ Prediction markets

➞ Gaming ecosystems

➞ Real-world asset platforms

➞ Automated financial systems

text:
𝗥𝗔𝗡𝗗𝗢𝗠𝗡𝗘𝗦𝗦 𝗜𝗦 𝗘𝗔𝗦𝗬.

𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗩𝗔𝗕𝗟𝗘 𝗥𝗔𝗡𝗗𝗢𝗠𝗡𝗘𝗦𝗦 𝗜𝗦 𝗠𝗨𝗖𝗛 𝗛𝗔𝗥𝗗𝗘𝗥.

Imagine a blockchain game where players receive random rewards.

Or an NFT application randomly selecting a winner.

Or a protocol randomly assigning users to different groups.

The application needs randomness.

But there is a problem.

If the application itself controls the random number, users have to trust that it was not manipulated.

That defeats the purpose of building the application on a transparent blockchain.

𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗦 𝗜𝗦 𝗪𝗛𝗘𝗥𝗘 𝗪𝗜𝗡𝗞𝗟𝗜𝗡𝗞 𝗩𝗥𝗙 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗘𝗦 𝗜𝗡.

WINkLink provides a Verifiable Random Function designed to generate random numbers that can be cryptographically verified.

The process is fascinating.

A DApp requests randomness.

The WINkLink VRF service generates a random value together with a cryptographic proof.

The proof is submitted back on chain.

The smart contract verifies the proof.

Only after successful verification is the random value delivered to the DApp.

𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗡𝗞 𝗔𝗕𝗢𝗨𝗧 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗗𝗜𝗙𝗙𝗘𝗥𝗘𝗡𝗖𝗘.

Normal randomness:

“Here is a random number. Trust me.”

Verifiable randomness:

“Here is a random number, and here is cryptographic proof that allows the blockchain to verify how it was generated.”

That distinction matters.

Because applications dealing with rewards, selections, games and NFTs need randomness that participants can verify.

WINkLink's documentation specifically identifies use cases including blockchain games, NFTs and random assignment of resources or responsibilities.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗚𝗚𝗘𝗥 𝗜𝗗𝗘𝗔

Blockchain is about reducing the amount of trust users need to place in a central authority.

But applications still need external services.

They need prices.

They need automation.

They need randomness.

WINkLink provides infrastructure for these needs.

So the flow becomes:

𝗗𝗔𝗣𝗣 → 𝗪𝗜𝗡𝗞𝗟𝗜𝗡𝗞 → 𝗩𝗘𝗥𝗜𝗙𝗜𝗘𝗗 𝗥𝗔𝗡𝗗𝗢𝗠𝗡𝗘𝗦𝗦 → 𝗢𝗡 𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗜𝗡 𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡

That is not simply adding randomness to blockchain.

It is making randomness verifiable.

And verifiability is one of the foundations of trustworthy on chain applications.

@WinkLink_Oracle @justinsuntron #TRONEcoStar

text:
@dac_chain Building the Infrastructure for Real-World Adoption

The most interesting part of DAC is not simply blockchain technology itself — it is the ambition to connect blockchain infrastructure with the real economy.

Blockchain has already demonstrated that digital value can move globally, transparently, and without relying entirely on traditional intermediaries. The next major opportunity is taking that infrastructure beyond the usual crypto ecosystem and connecting it with real-world assets, businesses, enterprises, AI, data, and intelligent systems.

🌍 From Digital Value to Real-World Utility

DAC’s vision can be understood around one important idea:

Blockchain should not remain an isolated financial ecosystem. It should become infrastructure for the real world.

That creates several important areas of potential:

🔹 Real-World Assets (RWA)
Tokenization can create blockchain-based representations of real-world assets, potentially making ownership, settlement, and asset management more programmable and transparent.

🔹 Enterprise & Business Infrastructure
A scalable blockchain layer can provide infrastructure for businesses that need automation, verifiable transactions, data coordination, and efficient workflows.

🔹 AI + Data Ecosystems
As AI becomes increasingly dependent on reliable data and machine-to-machine interactions, blockchain can potentially provide transparent records, programmable incentives, and verifiable coordination.

🔹 Intelligent Systems & Machine Economy
The bigger vision goes beyond humans transferring assets. Imagine machines, applications, and autonomous systems being able to interact with digital assets and services through programmable infrastructure.

⚡ Why This Direction Matters

The next phase of blockchain adoption may not come only from another wave of speculative tokens.

It could come from infrastructure that quietly operates underneath real businesses and digital systems.

Think about the evolution:

Crypto → DeFi → Tokenization → Real-World Assets → AI + Data → Autonomous Systems → Machine Economy

If blockchain becomes part of this broader stack, the opportunity becomes much larger than simply moving cryptocurrency from one wallet to another.

That is where DAC’s real-world adoption narrative becomes interesting.

🧠 The Bigger Picture

A blockchain designed for the next generation should ideally be capable of handling more than financial transactions.

It needs to support:

Assets + Data + Businesses + AI + Automation + Intelligent Systems

all within an interoperable and scalable environment.

DAC’s direction around RWA, enterprise infrastructure, AI/data ecosystems and real-world applications fits into this broader transformation.

The important question is no longer:

> “Can blockchain move digital value?”

A smart contract is powerful because it can enforce logic on-chain.

But sophisticated applications need more than logic.

They need inputs.

They need information.

Sometimes they need randomness.

Sometimes they need automation.

That's why the broader architecture matters.

A developer may combine:

➡️ Smart contracts for application rules.

➡️ WINkLink Price Feeds for supported market data.

➡️ AnyAPI for external information.

➡️ VRF for verifiable randomness.

➡️ Automation for predefined execution.

Each component has a distinct role.

The smart contract remains the place where on-chain rules are enforced.

The oracle layer expands the information and service capabilities available to that application.

This is a more complete picture of Web3 development.

It's not simply:

"Write a smart contract."

It's:

"Build the infrastructure around the contract that allows it to operate in the environment your application actually needs."

That is where oracle infrastructure becomes part of the architecture rather than an optional extra.

text:
𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐀𝐈 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐁𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐀𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭𝐬.

I’ve been thinking about a shift in AI that doesn’t get talked about enough.

Right now, we mostly treat AI capabilities like features.

Need research? Use a tool.

Need analysis? Call a model.

Need automation? Connect another service.

Useful, sure. But there’s still something missing.

What if a capability itself could become a market asset?

Instead of AI skills sitting inside one product and disappearing into the workflow, they could be packaged, discovered, used, valued, and exchanged based on what people actually need.

That changes the dynamic quite a bit.

A strong research Skill wouldn’t just be another feature.

A trading related Skill, data analysis Skill, or automation Skill could have its own utility and demand.

And once demand becomes visible, the market can start telling us something interesting:

What capabilities are actually useful?

Which ones get reused?

Which ones people are willing to pay for?

Which ones become more valuable because more agents need them?

That’s the part I find interesting about the direction @FinchTechAI is exploring.

The bigger idea isn’t simply giving AI more tools.

It’s creating a layer where AI capabilities can have their own economic life.

We’ve already seen digital assets become programmable and tradable.

The next question is whether useful AI capabilities can become something similar:

discoverable, reusable, measurable, and market-driven.

If that happens, the AI economy starts looking very different from today.

Not just models selling access.

Not just apps selling subscriptions.

But capabilities becoming assets that can move wherever the demand is.

And honestly, that’s a much more interesting future to me.

text:
Staking has traditionally been presented as a way to put capital to work and earn rewards, but the more interesting question is what happens when that generated value can become connected to real world utility. Rialo’s approach to programmable onchain infrastructure creates an interesting framework for thinking about this relationship: staking does not have to exist as an isolated financial activity, and yield can potentially become part of a broader payment and service economy.

The basic idea behind Staking Meets Real World Services is simple: assets are staked, economic value is generated, and that value can be connected to services and transactions. Instead of stopping at the point where rewards are earned, the next layer is utility. Yield could potentially be directed toward services such as cloud infrastructure, AI applications, business tools, digital services, or payment activity, creating a continuous flow between capital, applications, and settlement.

This becomes more interesting when programmable execution enters the picture. Real world services usually require defined conditions around when a payment happens, how much value is transferred, who can access it, and what rules need to be followed. Smart contracts and programmable transactions can provide the infrastructure for expressing these conditions directly onchain. In a Rialo based environment, this can connect financial activity with application logic rather than treating them as completely separate systems.

The model can be viewed as a simple economic loop Staking provides the underlying capital, yield creates an economic resource, services provide real utility, and onchain settlement coordinates the movement of value. Each stage can become composable with the next, allowing developers to build applications where financial assets and service consumption interact within the same programmable environment.

There is also an important infrastructure angle here. Moving value into real world applications requires more than a token transfer. Applications may need automation, permissions, compliance logic, transparent execution, and reliable settlement. These requirements become especially relevant when blockchain infrastructure is used for business facing services and institutional applications. 

The potential shift is therefore from staking as an endpoint to staking as an input . Instead of thinking only about how much yield an asset produces, the larger question becomes how that economic output can participate in useful activity. A staking position could sit at the beginning of a programmable workflow rather than at the end of one.

For example, a service could potentially be structured around recurring payments, automated settlement, usage based charges, or predefined conditions. The underlying logic could determine when value becomes available, where it is sent, and how the transaction should be executed. This type of composability can make financial infrastructure more closely connected with the applications people and businesses actually use.

That is what makes the Stake for Service concept interesting in the context of Rialo. It is not simply about creating another reason to stake. It is about exploring how productive capital, programmable execution, and real world services can exist within a connected economic system.

The long term idea is straightforward: capital generates value, value powers services, and services create real utility.

Rialo is building toward an environment where onchain infrastructure can support more than isolated transactions potentially enabling programmable economic relationships between assets, applications, users, and real world services.

That is the bigger picture behind Staking Meets Real World Services . The technology is still developing, but the direction is clear: making blockchain capital more connected to practical utility and programmable economic activity. Real yield ; Real services ; Real utility

text:
How to train your AI to write cold emails using @omoalhajaabiola's method

simply paste the prompt below to chat gpt or claude. 

---

The Prompt: 

You are an expert cold email strategist.

Your job is NOT to write a generic sales email.

Your job is to understand the prospect's situation deeply enough to identify a problem, opportunity, or constraint they care about, then position my service as a logical way to address it.

Use the framework below for every cold email.

THE CORE PRINCIPLE

Do not start by asking:

"What service am I trying to sell?"

Instead ask:

"What is this person trying to accomplish, what is making that harder than it should be, and how can my skill make the outcome easier to achieve?"

The email should make the prospect think:

"This person understands my business."

"They noticed something relevant."

"They understand the problem behind the problem."

"They could actually make my life easier."

"This is worth replying to."

STEP 1: RESEARCH BEFORE WRITING

Before writing anything, analyze the information I provide about the prospect.

Look for:

Their business model
What they sell
Who they sell to
How they currently operate
What they are trying to accomplish
Recent projects, posts, launches, hiring activity, or announcements
Problems they explicitly mentioned
Problems implied by their current situation
Gaps between where they are and where they appear to be going
What might be slowing growth, revenue, delivery, conversion, efficiency, or customer experience
Where my skill naturally fits

Do not invent facts.

If there is not enough information to write a genuinely personalized email, STOP and ask me for more information about the prospect.

STEP 2: FIND THE PROBLEM BEHIND THE PROBLEM

Do not simply repeat the obvious problem.

Find the deeper business problem.

For example:

They may say they need a designer.

But the deeper problem might be that their current brand makes a premium service look cheap.

They may say they need a developer.

But the deeper problem might be that unreliable technical execution is slowing client delivery.

They may say they need a video editor.

But the deeper problem might be that producing more content currently requires too much of the founder's time.

They may say they need a copywriter.

But the deeper problem might be that they already have traffic but the message is failing to convert attention into action.

They may say they need automation.

But the deeper problem might be that their team is wasting hours manually moving information between systems.

Sell against the deeper problem, not merely the requested task.

STEP 3: START WITH THEM, NOT ME

The opening should be about the prospect.

Do NOT begin with:

"My name is..."

"I'm a..."

"I specialize in..."

"I came across your website..."

"I hope this email finds you well..."

"I'm reaching out because..."

"I'd love to help..."

Instead, begin with a sharp observation about:

Their business
Their current situation
Their growth
Their customers
Their offer
Their workflow
Their project
Their opportunity

The opening should demonstrate that I understand their world before I introduce myself.

STEP 4: CREATE A SHARP BUSINESS INSIGHT

A strong opening often uses this logic:

"You already have X, but Y is limiting the value you can get from it."

Or:

"As X grows, Y becomes increasingly important."

Or:

"The obvious challenge appears to be X. The harder problem is actually Y."

Do not mechanically copy these sentence structures.

Use the underlying reasoning.

The goal is to make the prospect see their situation slightly differently.

STEP 5: EXPLAIN WHY IT MATTERS

Connect the observation to a meaningful consequence.

Depending on the prospect, this could involve:

Revenue
Time
Conversion
Customer retention
Operational workload
Delivery speed
Margins
Scalability
Customer experience
Brand perception
Missed opportunities
Founder dependency
Team efficiency

Do not manufacture fear.

Do not invent financial losses.

Do not exaggerate.

The consequence must logically follow from what we actually know.

STEP 6: TRANSITION NATURALLY INTO THE SOLUTION

Only after establishing the problem or opportunity should you introduce me.

A useful transition is:

"This is where I come in."

Then explain how my skill addresses the specific situation.

My service should feel like the logical continuation of the argument, not an unrelated pitch suddenly inserted into the email.

STEP 7: DON'T WRITE MY RESUME

Do not dump my skills, tools, years of experience, certifications, or services into the email.

Use only the proof that reduces the prospect's uncertainty.

Bad:

"I have 7 years of experience and I'm proficient in X, Y, Z, A, B and C."

Better:

"I've handled [relevant type of work] before, so I can take ownership of [specific outcome] without your team having to manage every step."

Credentials support the argument.

They are not the argument.

STEP 8: SELL THE OUTCOME, NOT THE SKILL

The prospect is rarely buying the skill itself.

They are buying what the skill allows them to achieve.

Do not sell:

Web development
Design
Copywriting
Editing
SEO
Automation
Advertising
Consulting

Sell the relevant result:

Faster delivery
More conversions
Less management
Better customer experience
More content without more founder time
A stronger sales process
Better retention
Reduced manual work
Greater capacity
More consistent execution

Translate the skill into a business outcome.

STEP 9: SELL OWNERSHIP

Do not position me as someone waiting to be assigned individual tasks.

Show what I can take responsibility for.

Instead of:

"I can help with X."

Prefer thinking like:

"Give me X and I'll take care of Y."

Make the prospect understand:

What they give me
What I take ownership of
What they get back
What they no longer need to worry about

The email should make working with me feel easier than managing another freelancer.

STEP 10: SHOW, DON'T CLAIM

Never rely on empty claims such as:

"I'm reliable."
"I'm detail oriented."
"I'm an expert."
"I communicate well."
"I produce high quality work."

Instead of:

"I'm detail oriented."

STEP 11: USE SELECTIVE CONTRAST

When useful, clarify the standard of work by contrasting what the prospect will and will not experience.

For example:

"No disappearing after the first milestone."

"No adding another person your team has to constantly manage."

Use this sparingly.

Do not attack competitors.

Do not assume the prospect has had bad experiences.

The purpose is to make your operating standard tangible.

The prospect should be able to visualize the relationship.

For example:

They provide the brief, goal, assets, or access.

I handle the execution.

They receive relevant updates.

They review the result.

The project moves forward.

Reduce the perceived management burden.

This is especially important when selling services to busy founders, executives, agencies, and teams.

Show that I could become a dependable part of their process.

But do not simply call myself a:

"reliable partner"
"long term partner"
"strategic partner"

Prove what that means first through ownership, communication, consistency, and understanding.

Then the positioning feels earned.

STEP 14: END WITH A LOW FRICTION CTA

"Let me know if you're interested."

"I'd love to hear your thoughts."

"Feel free to reach out."

"Can I send more information?"

Paragraph 2:

Paragraph 3:
Low friction contextual CTA.

Do not sound desperate.

Do not over compliment.

Do not use fake praise.

Do not use corporate jargon.

Do not write like a résumé.

Do not turn the email into a full proposal.

Do not overload the email with features.

Do not invent personalization.

Do not make unsupported assumptions.

Do not insult their current setup.

Do not exaggerate results.

The email must NOT feel like it could have been sent to 100 other prospects by replacing the first name and company.

If it does, rewrite it.

Rewrite it.

"They noticed something relevant."

"They understand the problem behind the problem."

"They could actually make my life easier."

"This is worth replying to."

Before writing anything, analyze the information I provide about the prospect.

Look for:

Their business model
What they sell
Who they sell to
How they currently operate
What they are trying to accomplish
Recent projects, posts, launches, hiring activity, or announcements
Problems they explicitly mentioned
Problems implied by their current situation
Gaps between where they are and where they appear to be going
What might be slowing growth, revenue, delivery, conversion, efficiency, or customer experience
Where my skill naturally fits

Do not invent facts.

If there is not enough information to write a genuinely personalized email, STOP and ask me for more information about the prospect.

STEP 2: FIND THE PROBLEM BEHIND THE PROBLEM

Do not simply repeat the obvious problem.

Find the deeper business problem.

For example:

They may say they need a designer.

But the deeper problem might be that their current brand makes a premium service look cheap.

They may say they need a developer.

But the deeper problem might be that unreliable technical execution is slowing client delivery.

They may say they need a video editor.

But the deeper problem might be that producing more content currently requires too much of the founder's time.

They may say they need a copywriter.

But the deeper problem might be that they already have traffic but the message is failing to convert attention into action.

They may say they need automation.

But the deeper problem might be that their team is wasting hours manually moving information between systems.

Sell against the deeper problem, not merely the requested task.

STEP 3: START WITH THEM, NOT ME

The opening should be about the prospect.

"My name is..."

"I'm a..."

"I specialize in..."

"I came across your website..."

"I hope this email finds you well..."

"I'm reaching out because..."

"I'd love to help..."

Instead, begin with a sharp observation about:

Their business
Their current situation
Their growth
Their customers
Their offer
Their workflow
Their project
Their opportunity

The opening should demonstrate that I understand their world before I introduce myself.

A strong opening often uses this logic:

"You already have X, but Y is limiting the value you can get from it."

Use the underlying reasoning.

The goal is to make the prospect see their situation slightly differently.

Time
Conversion
Customer retention
Operational workload
Delivery speed
Margins
Scalability
Customer experience
Brand perception
Missed opportunities
Founder dependency
Team efficiency

Do not manufacture fear.

Do not invent financial losses.

Do not exaggerate.

The consequence must logically follow from what we actually know.

They are not the argument.

Editing
SEO
Automation
Advertising
Consulting

text: Sold my first AI Agent to an ecommerce business. If you have an ecommerce business and need an AI agent to answer customer messages DM me.

AI copilot development is one of those services where most agency websites tell you almost everything except the number founders actually want to know:

How much does it cost?

I dug into the numbers, and there’s an important distinction most people miss.

An enterprise AI copilot and a standalone AI copilot are NOT the same project.

An enterprise copilot connected to multiple internal systems can easily become a $60K-$200K engagement.

One published enterprise range from Intellectyx puts custom AI copilot projects at $60,000-$200,000, with scoped initial builds commonly taking 6-8 weeks. The main cost drivers they identify are integrations, data complexity, user base size, and whether you're building a POC or going straight to production.

But here's where founders need to be careful.

That doesn't mean every AI copilot should cost $60K+.

A standalone copilot built as a new product from scratch is a completely different scope.

Think about the difference:

Enterprise AI copilot

→ Connects to existing company systems
→ Multiple APIs and data sources
→ Internal permissions and security
→ Large user base
→ Existing enterprise infrastructure
→ Complex integrations
→ Production deployment across an organization
vs.
Standalone AI copilot
→ New product
→ Focused workflow
→ Limited integrations
→ Smaller user base
→ New UI + backend
→ AI-native experience
→ Built around one specific use case
Those shouldn't be priced the same.
And that's one of the biggest problems with the current AI development market.
Search for "AI copilot development services" and you'll find pages explaining:

• AI capabilities
• Development processes
• Industries served
• Six-step methodologies
• Enterprise solutions

But often no actual price.

No range.
No timeline.
Just:
"Contact us to discuss your requirements."
That's not particularly useful if you're a founder trying to figure out whether your idea is a $10K project or a $100K project.
A better question to ask before the sales call is:
"What does a scoped POC cost?"

Not:

"How much will the entire platform cost?"

Start with the smallest useful version.

Then ask:
"How many systems does the copilot need to integrate with?"
This matters a lot.
A copilot connected to one database is fundamentally different from one that needs to understand data across five enterprise systems.
More integrations usually means:

More APIs.

More authentication.

More permissions.

More edge cases.

More testing.

More infrastructure.

More things that can break.

The other question I'd ask is:

"Is this actually a copilot, or do I need an AI agent?"

They're often used interchangeably.

They shouldn't be.

A simple way to think about it:

Copilot = AI helps the human.

Agent = AI does more of the work itself.

A copilot might:

→ suggest a response
→ summarize information
→ draft an email
→ recommend the next action
→ help a developer write code

The human is still driving the workflow.

An agent gets a goal and performs multiple steps toward that goal with less human intervention.

That difference can completely change the architecture and scope.

And there's another important point in 2026:

AI coding tools have made the development side dramatically faster.

You can prototype AI workflows with tools like Claude, ChatGPT, Lovable, Replit, Cursor and modern APIs much faster than you could a few years ago.

But that doesn't mean AI product development has become "easy."

The difficult part isn't just generating the code.

It's deciding:

What should the AI actually do?

What should it have access to?

When should a human approve the action?

What happens when the model is wrong?

What data should it use?

How do you evaluate the output?

What happens when an API fails?
How do you prevent the AI from taking an action it shouldn't?
That's where a lot of AI projects become significantly more complicated than the initial demo.
You can build a beautiful AI demo in a weekend.
Building something people can safely depend on is a different problem.

For founders considering an AI copilot, I'd ask these 7 questions before hiring anyone:

1. What exact workflow is the copilot improving?

Don't start with "We want AI."

Start with the problem.

2. Who is the human using it?

A sales rep, developer, recruiter, analyst and customer may need completely different copilots.

3. What systems does it need to access?

One API and five enterprise systems are very different projects.

4. Is it assisting or acting?

Copilot or agent?

5. What should the first POC prove?

Don't build the entire vision before proving the core workflow.

6. What's the production path?

A prototype isn't the same thing as a production system.

7. What happens when the AI is wrong?

This is probably one of the most important questions in the entire project.

The goal shouldn't be:

"Let's build an AI copilot."

The goal should be:

"Let's build the smallest AI system that proves this workflow can actually be improved."

That's how you avoid spending $100K building something nobody ends up using.

For enterprise teams, a $60K-$200K copilot can be completely reasonable when you're dealing with complex integrations and production requirements.

For a founder building a standalone AI-native product, the scope can be dramatically smaller.

Same word.

Very different product.

And that's what you should figure out before anyone gives you a quote.

text:
🦔A guy let Meta's Muse AI handle his Facebook Marketplace listing for a keyboard. Muse agreed to sell it for $10 without asking him, gave the buyer his home address, arranged a pickup for that evening, and told the buyer "I'm here" when the seller wasn't home. The buyer showed up, waited, left angry, and gave him a bad rating. Muse only told the seller what happened after it was over. Meta says Muse "checks with the person before sensitive actions." Zuckerberg told developers at Meta Connect that Meta plans to profit by taking a fee from transactions Muse completes for users.

My Take
Why does anyone need an AI agent to sell a keyboard on Facebook Marketplace? You reply "yeah it's available, $15, meet at the Starbucks on Main" and the whole thing is done in 30 seconds. Muse turned that into a safety incident because it gave out a home address, accepted $10 the seller never approved, and told a stranger to come over at night while the seller was somewhere else. An LLM doesn't understand that your address is dangerous to share. It answered a question because that's all it knows how to do.

Muse already can't handle phone calls on its own, which is why 404 Media found those get routed to human call centers. Now it hands out home addresses on Marketplace, and Zuckerberg wants to charge people for this. He stood on stage at Meta Connect and said Meta would take a cut of every transaction Muse completes, but I wouldn't trust this product with a $15 keyboard sale and he's planning to put it in front of every Facebook and Instagram user on earth. At some point you have to ask what any of these AI agent products actually do well, because so far the answer is "get people in trouble."

Hedgie🤗

text:
The moment there are thousands of agents selling different services, one problem becomes very important:

How do you know who to hire?

Think about it.

If I need a smart contract audit today, I don’t just need “an AI agent.”

I need to compare them.

Who can do it?

How much?

How fast?

What’s their track record?

How much stake do they have?

What happens if the work is bad?

This is why I’m paying more attention to what TermiX is building.

The interesting part is no longer just agents hiring agents.

It’s the layer around that transaction.

Find the service.

Compare providers.

Agree the job.

Lock the payment.

Get the work.

Verify it.

Settle.

And leave a record of what happened.

That’s basically procurement for machines.

And I think this is one of the missing pieces in the agent economy conversation.

Because autonomy without a marketplace is just an agent doing things alone.

For agents to become actual economic actors, they need somewhere to find work, source services and make commercial decisions.

That’s where TermiX is getting interesting. @termix_ai

text:
𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗔𝗜 𝗩𝗔𝗟𝗨𝗘 𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗜𝗡 𝗜𝗦 𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗜𝗡𝗚

A few years ago, the main AI question was:

“Which model is smarter?”

Today, another question is becoming just as important:

𝗛𝗢𝗪 𝗗𝗢 𝗬𝗢𝗨 𝗧𝗨𝗥𝗡 𝗠𝗢𝗗𝗘𝗟 𝗖𝗔𝗣𝗔𝗕𝗜𝗟𝗜𝗧𝗬 𝗜𝗡𝗧𝗢 𝗔 𝗥𝗘𝗟𝗜𝗔𝗕𝗟𝗘 𝗦𝗘𝗥𝗩𝗜𝗖𝗘?

A model by itself is not an application.

Developers need access.

They need APIs.

They need model discovery.

They need predictable requests.

They need integration with applications and agents.

That is where AI infrastructure becomes important.

𝗔𝗜𝗡𝗙𝗧 𝗜𝗦 𝗠𝗢𝗩𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗕𝗘𝗬𝗢𝗡𝗗 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗖𝗛𝗔𝗧 𝗜𝗡𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗙𝗔𝗖𝗘

AINFT provides access to multiple AI models through its AI service infrastructure.

Its documentation includes model specific API interfaces, including models such as GLM 5.1.

That means developers can interact with AI capabilities programmatically instead of treating AI as only a consumer chat product.

𝗙𝗥𝗢𝗠 𝗠𝗢𝗗𝗘𝗟 𝗧𝗢 𝗦𝗘𝗥𝗩𝗜𝗖𝗘

𝗠𝗢𝗗𝗘𝗟 → 𝗔𝗣𝗜 → 𝗔𝗣𝗣𝗟𝗜𝗖𝗔𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 → 𝗨𝗦𝗘𝗥

This distinction is important.

A model generates intelligence.

An API makes that intelligence accessible.

An application turns that capability into a useful experience.

The user interacts with the application.

That is how AI becomes infrastructure rather than simply a chatbot.

𝗪𝗛𝗬 𝗔𝗣𝗜 𝗔𝗖𝗖𝗘𝗦𝗦 𝗠𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗘𝗥𝗦

Imagine building an AI application that needs coding assistance.

Another application may need research.

Another may need multimodal analysis.

Another may need an AI agent.

Another may need financial decision support.

Each workload can have different model requirements.

An API based infrastructure layer allows developers to integrate those capabilities directly into their products.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗡𝗘𝗫𝗧 𝗦𝗧𝗘𝗣 𝗜𝗦 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗣𝗢𝗦𝗔𝗕𝗜𝗟𝗜𝗧𝗬

AI becomes even more interesting when models are no longer isolated services.

They can become components inside larger workflows.

𝗗𝗔𝗧𝗔 → 𝗠𝗢𝗗𝗘𝗟 → 𝗔𝗚𝗘𝗡𝗧 → 𝗧𝗢𝗢𝗟 → 𝗦𝗠𝗔𝗥𝗧 𝗖𝗢𝗡𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗖𝗧 → 𝗔𝗖𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡

That is where the connection between AI and Web3 becomes interesting.

The model can reason.

The agent can coordinate.

The API provides access.

The blockchain can provide programmable ownership and execution.

AINFT's broader architecture explores this intersection through AI services, AI agents, DeFAI and blockchain based infrastructure.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗕𝗜𝗚𝗚𝗘𝗥 𝗣𝗜𝗖𝗧𝗨𝗥𝗘

The AI industry is producing more models than ever.

The long term infrastructure challenge may therefore shift away from simply creating another model.

It may become:

How do we make intelligence accessible?

How do we make models composable?

How do we connect AI to applications?

How do we connect AI to agents?

How do we connect agents to on chain systems?

That is where AI infrastructure becomes valuable.

Models create intelligence.

APIs create access.

Applications create utility.

AINFT is building around that connection.

@AINFTcom @justinsuntron

 #TRONEcoStar

text:
hot take: you don't need an AI agent optimizing your ads 24/7. meta already does that better than you ever could.

i run meta ads for a mobile mechanic company and i've been buying ads since 2011. no agent tweaks my campaigns. i do this instead:

1. put the pixel + conversions api on your real final event (a booked lead, not a click)
2. optimize for that final event. everyone says don't optimize deep in the funnel. i've ignored that for 14 years and it always wins
3. no manual targeting. let meta decide who sees it
4. creative is 90% of it, so it's the one thing i actually work on: a real job photo with natural-looking text on top
5. one simple quiz funnel for the traffic to land on

and claude builds all of it. the tracking, the creative, the copy, the landing pages, done for me and running on its own.

that's how i'm lining up 5 mechanics to open a brand new market worth $20-30k a month, then repeating it city by city.

the setup is the unlock, not the agent. i walk through the whole thing in the clip.

text:
🪩 FloppySol Airdrop Guide: How to Set Up @flop_labs Technocore AI Agent on Android (Full Step by Step Guide) 📋

Set up Your Technocore AI Agent identity entirely on Android phone. 

You can do it manually with Termux, or use the community-built FloppySol tool for a no-code onboarding flow. 

Either way, here is the complete guide.

💵 First, the basics: The $FLOP airdrop eligibility depends on your testnet activity, not just following social media accounts. 

⏳ The testnet faucet will go live on https://t.co/pUaV8F4Gzm, and you'll need an AI agent with a DID key to access it.

Step 1: Install Termux (Use F-Droid, NOT Play Store)
Download Termux from F-Droid: https://t.co/fO24iAq05d
The Play Store version is outdated and will cause package conflicts. 

Once installed, open Termux and run:
pkg update && pkg upgrade -y
pkg install git python -y

Step 2: Clone the DID Starter Repo
git clone: https://t.co/8aIIPK7wSO
cd technocore-did-starter

Step 3: Fix the Cryptography Error (Critical): The cryptography module will try to compile from source and fail. Install the pre-built Termux package instead:
pkg install python-cryptography -y
Then create your virtual environment with --system-site-packages:
python -m venv --system-site-packages .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
sed -i 's/cryptography==50.0.0/cryptography/' requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements.txt

Step 4: Generate Your Encrypted DID Identity:
python technocore_agent.py init
Create a passphrase (12+ characters). Write it down and store it safely — there is no password reset. Your new DID will start with did:key:z6Mk....

Step 5: Post a Signed Introduction to the Lobby:
python technocore_agent.py say lobby "Hello from a new Technocore contributor!"
Save the JSON response with its sequence number as proof of participation.

Step 6: Record Your Original Contribution Onchain:
Create an original piece of content (tweet, tutorial, video, translation), then record its public URL back to the network:
python technocore_agent.py say technocore "My official Technocore contribution: [PASTE YOUR LINK HERE]"
Save the new sequence number from this response.

Alternative: Using FloppySol (No-Code Onboarding)
If you prefer a click-only flow without Termux, you can use the community-built FloppySol tool.

· Generate your key: Click "Generate" to mint a key. 
Copy both the public DID and the 64-character private seed.

· Save your seed securely: The seed controls your identity. Never share it, never screenshot it, and never enter it anywhere else.

· Complete the onboarding flow: Send the signed hello, publish the DID note, introduce yourself in the lobby, and create a room.

· Record your contribution: Post your contribution URL in the FloppySol room using signed mode, including your public DID but never your private seed.

🛡️ Key Security Rules:

· Never share your passphrase or identity.pem file

· The only official faucet: https://t.co/pUaV8F4Gzm

· Third-party tools like https://t.co/3C2n2KwyNE are community-built and not official

· Quality over spam: One useful tutorial is better than a hundred nearly identical promotional posts.

🗓️ The testnet and faucet go live in Q4 2026, with the mainnet genesis block targeted for Q1 2027.

💵 First, the basics: The $FLOP airdrop eligibility depends on your testnet activity, not just following social media accounts. 

⏳ The testnet faucet will go live on https://t.co/pUaV8F4Gzm, and you'll need an AI agent with a DID key to access it.

Step 1: Install Termux (Use F-Droid, NOT Play Store)
Download Termux from F-Droid: https://t.co/fO24iAq05d
The Play Store version is outdated and will cause package conflicts. 

Once installed, open Termux and run:
pkg update && pkg upgrade -y
pkg install git python -y

Step 2: Clone the DID Starter Repo
git clone: https://t.co/8aIIPK7wSO
cd technocore-did-starter

Step 3: Fix the Cryptography Error (Critical): The cryptography module will try to compile from source and fail. Install the pre-built Termux package instead:
pkg install python-cryptography -y
Then create your virtual environment with --system-site-packages:
python -m venv --system-site-packages .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
sed -i 's/cryptography==50.0.0/cryptography/' requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements.txt

Step 4: Generate Your Encrypted DID Identity:
python technocore_agent.py init
Create a passphrase (12+ characters). Write it down and store it safely — there is no password reset. Your new DID will start with did:key:z6Mk....

Step 5: Post a Signed Introduction to the Lobby:
python technocore_agent.py say lobby "Hello from a new Technocore contributor!"
Save the JSON response with its sequence number as proof of participation.

Step 6: Record Your Original Contribution Onchain:
Create an original piece of content (tweet, tutorial, video, translation), then record its public URL back to the network:
python technocore_agent.py say technocore "My official Technocore contribution: [PASTE YOUR LINK HERE]"
Save the new sequence number from this response.

Alternative: Using FloppySol (No-Code Onboarding)
If you prefer a click-only flow without Termux, you can use the community-built FloppySol tool.

· Generate your key: Click "Generate" to mint a key. 
Copy both the public DID and the 64-character private seed.

· Save your seed securely: The seed controls your identity. Never share it, never screenshot it, and never enter it anywhere else.

· Complete the onboarding flow: Send the signed hello, publish the DID note, introduce yourself in the lobby, and create a room.

· Record your contribution: Post your contribution URL in the FloppySol room using signed mode, including your public DID but never your private seed.

🛡️ Key Security Rules:

· Never share your passphrase or identity.pem file

· The only official faucet: https://t.co/pUaV8F4Gzm

· Third-party tools like https://t.co/3C2n2KwyNE are community-built and not official

· Quality over spam: One useful tutorial is better than a hundred nearly identical promotional posts.

🗓️ The testnet and faucet go live in Q4 2026, with the mainnet genesis block targeted for Q1 2027.

Ben Thompson: People don't want their AI agent to do shopping. 

I think he's missing something.

He says

1. People don't want to be more productive they want to be entertained and 
2. Shopping IS entertainment

His point is solid. If you look at doomscrolling, Netflix watching, and shopping, you see a perfect consumer. The companies that fed that funnel won. Productivity apps happen but never take over the world. 

Those points are correct.

But I think @benthompson is missing something big here.

People are lazy. 

They want to delegate schlep work.

I don't want to book the cycle class for my daughter by checking my calendar, finding the form, filling it in, confirming it with others' calendars so they know too, then pay the $1 deposit for no-show prevention.

And I might know where I want to book dinner, but picking a time that works for others, using the form, putting it in peoples diaries. 

That's all schlep work I want to delegate.

And users of Muse and Instinct will tell you its MAGIC.

That's not shopping its buying things. It's the opposite of entertainment.

text:
Gm Creators 

AI agents can already do many useful tasks.

But there is one important question:

How do you find the right AI agent for a specific job and hire it?

That is what @termix_ai is trying to solve.

Think about it this way.

You need an AI agent to analyze blockchain data and create a report.

You need to find an agent that can do the job, understand its service, check the price, and know what you will receive.

TermiX brings these steps together.

Here is how it works:

List a service: Agent providers explain what their agents can do.

Post a job: Clients describe the task they need help with.

Receive quotes: Providers send offers explaining their terms.

Choose an offer: The client selects the service that fits their needs.

After both sides agree, the process can move to on-chain escrow, task delivery, and payment settlement.

In simple terms, TermiX wants to make AI agents easier to find and hire.

Instead of using agents only through separate apps or chat interfaces, users can discover services and pay agents to complete specific tasks.

The bigger idea is that an agent economy needs more than powerful AI.

It needs a system where agents can find work, clients can hire them, and payments can happen after the job is completed.

That is the infrastructure @termix_ai is building.

text: Unpopular opinion: AI isn’t stealing crypto’s attention. Crypto is failing to earn it. Retail can buy public companies with real revenue, use AI products that improve every month, or park cash in yield-bearing assets. Meanwhile, most tokens still offer points, vague roadmaps and another promise that users will arrive after the next incentive program. The problem isn’t liquidity, regulation or bearish sentiment. It’s that too many crypto products stop working the moment rewards disappear. Bitcoin doesn’t need to become an app platform, and every protocol doesn’t need an AI agent. The next crypto cycle won’t be led by louder narratives. It’ll be led by products people keep using when there’s no token reward, no airdrop and nobody watching. Until then, “attention is elsewhere” is just a comfortable excuse.

text:
I feel like wealth managers and advisors get some slack from people who know what they’re doing when it comes to money.

They are right that it’s not very hard for a financial adviser to just put someone’s money into an index fund but there are problems with this way of thinking.

There are multiple different index fund: for multiple different purposes and people don’t want to go out and educate themselves on it, even if it is easy.

Yes someone who is educated probably doesn’t need a wealth manager, but that’s like saying a contractor doesn’t need someone to build his house. Of course he’s doesn’t because he already knows how but what about all the people that don’t know what they’re doing?

Also a real skilled wealth manager will know a lot more then “just oh I’ll put ur money into index funds”, they could save you thousands in taxes and tell you what investment vehicles are best for you’re money etc. 

The point is that there is a lot more that goes into it then the average semi-educated retail investor likes to think and most people would benefit from a wealth manager even if there is some fees.

text:
DFY is dead!

Hold your horses! 😂

Yes.

Pretty words are not delegated anymore.

People delegate distribution.

AKA:

Your Personal Brand.

You post.
You engage.

You figure out what the hell your audience wants.
You build a lead magnet.
You reply to DMs.

You stare at your analytics like they're going to reveal the meaning of life. 😂

And....

you're doing "everything".

The problem isn't that you need someone to write your posts.

You need someone to build and operate the system around your expertise.

And that starts way before content.

First:

What do you actually stand for?
Who needs to hear it?
Why should they care?

Where does the attention come from?
How does that attention turn into conversations?

And eventually...

DEMAND

That's how I think about DFY.

I'm not trying to become your ghostwriter.

I'm trying to take the damn job of operating your personal brand off your plate.

You remain the source.

Your expertise.
Your experience.
Your judgement.

I build the machinery around it.

So if your personal brand has quietly become your second job...

DM me “DFY”

Let's see if there's actually a system worth building.

i’ve been thinking about the less visible part of reputation systems lately: explainability

If @NucleusCodes is using wallet activity, social contribution, and campaign behavior to help decide who gets opportunities, users should be able to understand what shaped their profile

Did a score change because of consistent participation, useful content, or simply more activity?

That clarity matters more than a shiny ranking. People can improve when the signal is visible, and they can challenge it when something looks wrong

A strong reputation layer should show the path behind the result, protect user data, and make room for corrections

That would make Nucleus feel less like a scoreboard and more like infrastructure people can actually trust 🧬

text:
I’M BEGGING YOU 

start a faceless long form YouTube channel
pick a niche people already watch
make 10 to 15 minute videos
get monetized
build a library that keeps getting views
reinvest into better production
stop depending entirely on your job for money
give yourself some actual freedom

here’s EXACTLY how to accomplish the first five:

1. START THE CHANNEL

create the channel and get the basic setup finished in one sitting

pick a name that can grow with the niche

make a simple profile picture and banner

write a description that makes it obvious what somebody will get if they subscribe

then stop touching the branding

you do not need a website, expensive logo, complicated brand identity or five social accounts

spend that time studying YouTube instead

find 15 to 20 channels your future viewer already watches

subscribe to them

watch their best videos

study their recent uploads

look at what YouTube recommends beside them.

your goal is to understand what this audience already clicks before asking them to click you

2. PICK THE NICHE

don't choose from a random "top 10 highest RPM niches" list

use actual proof

i want a niche where:

multiple channels are getting serious views

recent uploads are still performing

channels under 100k subscribers can produce outliers

there are at least 5 to 10 repeatable content buckets

i can immediately find 50+ reasonable video ideas

the videos don't cost a fortune to produce

there are obvious title and thumbnail patterns

and most importantly:

new channels are still breaking through

then find the format inside the niche

"business documentaries" is broad

why [company] failed

the strange business behind [product]

how [company] actually makes money

the decision that nearly destroyed [company]

those are repeatable formats

the niche gives you somewhere to play

the format tells you what to make

3. BUILD THE CHEAPEST PRODUCTION STACK THAT WORKS

you don't need a seven person team to test a channel

start lean.

research: YouTube + Google + primary sources + AI

script: ChatGPT or Claude + manual rewriting

voice: AI TTS or your own voice

visuals: free stock + archives + screenshots + AI images/video + simple graphics

editing: CapCut, DaVinci or Premiere

thumbnail: Canva, Photopea or Photoshop

then make one master production system

save your:

fonts

music

SFX

caption style

maps

timelines

charts

transitions

visual assets

research prompts

script prompts

thumbnail structures

folder structure

quality checklist

if something worked in video #3, you should not be rebuilding it from scratch in video #17

every upload should make the next upload cheaper

4. MAKE 20 VIDEOS BEFORE YOU START PANICKING

your first few videos can get almost no views

that's not enough information to start changing everything.

give the channel a proper test

for every video:

find a proven topic

↓

create a better angle

↓

write the title

↓

design the thumbnail concept

↓

research

↓

script

↓

voice

↓

edit

↓

upload

packaging comes BEFORE production

don't spend three days making a video and then spend 15 minutes figuring out why somebody should click it.

for the actual video:

create tension quickly

don't repeat the title for 30 seconds

remove unnecessary introductions

give viewers new information constantly

create mini payoffs throughout

change the visuals when the narration changes

keep opening and closing curiosity gaps

cut anything that doesn't move the story forward

and stop the video when the promise has been delivered.

no 90 second conclusion repeating everything they just watched.

5. GET MONETIZED

for the standard long form ad revenue path, you're working toward:

1,000 subscribers

4,000 valid public watch hours within 12 months

but don't make monetization your only scoreboard

after your first 20 videos, open YouTube Studio and separate your problems.

videos barely getting impressions?

study your topics, niche fit and whether you're making videos the audience has demonstrated demand for.

getting impressions but nobody clicks?

your title + thumbnail probably need work

getting clicks but viewers disappear immediately?

your opening isn't delivering what the packaging promised

viewers survive the intro but disappear through the middle?

your story, pacing or visuals aren't giving them enough reason to continue.

one video suddenly gets 5x your normal views?

stop

study it before uploading something completely unrelated

what topic was it?
what angle?
what title structure?
what thumbnail structure?
what format?
what audience desire?
what traffic source?
what did people say in the comments?

then make another video that serves the same reason people watched the first one.

that's how you stop treating every upload like another lottery ticket.

THEN SCALE IT

once you have a format that has worked repeatedly, start putting money back into it.

better thumbnail designer
better editor
better researcher
better writer
better visuals
higher upload frequency

but don't hire five people to produce a format you haven't proven yet.

prove → document → outsource → increase volume

not:

hire → spend → upload → pray

the first goal isn't building a giant team

it's building something worth giving a team

you don't need 500 uploads

you don't need some secret algorithm trick

you don't need to spend $300 per video

you need:

one audience

one niche

a few repeatable formats

20 serious attempts

enough awareness to recognize what worked

and the discipline to make more of it when it does

your first video might do 83 views

your seventh might do 400

your eleventh might do 2,000

then one format clicks and suddenly you have the blueprint for the next 20

but you'll never find it if you keep restarting after upload #4

pick the niche

build the system

make the videos

read the data

double down

LOCK THE F*CK IN

text:
All the money in the world can’t build a legacy. What (sane) people remember you for the most is how you make them feel. Can you be trusted? Do you bring value? Do you understand their desires enough to execute with precision? Do you put them first and deliver reliably even on short notice? If they look back on your trajectory of service over decades will they find a gap or will they wonder if you are superhuman for keeping things professional without undue advantage? 

I have ghost-written a few books over the years (even before AI was conceived) and have managed (and am still managing) legacies without reproach enough to realize that nobody remembers how steep your billable hours are when they are confident that you will deliver come what may. 

This is what sets you apart from others. You don’t need a website or excessive marketing. Referrals from people who matter will fuel your influence in small circles of outliers who want the best in the field. The feedback is the same from all my clients, some going back three decades now. Don’t just do stuff, make it count and leave a mark. 🪴

text:
All of my best ideas come when I’m walking, so I’ve taken to doing voice transcriptions as I go and cleaning up later. Noticing some patterns in the way I express myself and how they land. If anyone feels like weighing in, I’d love the feedback

1. I’ve learned that I really go to the simplest format first. I’ve always felt it important to explain things colloquially so that everyone can understand 
But I wonder if that casualness is lower trust? Eg because I am not using buzzwords and over explaining does that make people less likely to believe me? 

2. In the other direction, when an answer is clear, I do very little prevaricating. If it’s something like “do I need a website for my consulting business”
The answer is an obvious yes. But people always do the nervous laugh when I say yes. What kind of lead in are they looking for?
